name: Horundar
known_status: One of the twenty-two imprisoned gods of Universal. Able to influence worshippers through sanctioned rites, dreams, omens, miracles, cults, and the institutions that maintain the divine prisons.
manifestation: Horundar’s body leaks vapor, ash, seawater, or dust depending on emotional state.
deity_description: In the mythic structure of Universal, Horundar is not merely the god of seas, storms, earthquakes, and horses but a primal sovereign of oceanic dominion embedded within a predatory divine hierarchy that feeds upon mortal existence. Within the celestial order, he stands among the upper divine castes, ruling vast submerged citadels and storm-wracked coastal thrones, his authority stretching across every oceanic boundary that separates civilizations. Though not one of the ultimate High Fathers, his domain is so vast and uncontrollable that entire coastal kingdoms exist only under conditional survival, perpetually aware that the sea itself is not an indifferent force but a living, hungry extension of his will.

Horundar’s nature is volatile, proud, and deeply reactive, and in Universal theology his emotions are not symbolic but literal forces of reality. His rage becomes storm systems, tidal annihilations, and seismic ruptures that are interpreted as sacramental catastrophes rather than natural disasters. Shipwrecks and drowned cities are not accidents but curated harvests, moments where mortal life is collected through the ocean as offerings to divine appetite. His trident is both a symbol of sovereignty and a ritual instrument that “opens” the sea, allowing him to draw life essence from those lost beneath the waves. To sailors and coastal priests, calm seas represent temporary satisfaction, while storms signal an active feeding cycle in which the ocean becomes both temple and execution ground.

Within Universal cosmology, Horundar’s influence is inseparable from the wider divine economy of consumption that defines the pantheon. The gods are not sustained by faith alone but by the extraction of mortal essence through prayer, sacrifice, emotion, and suffering. Temples function as conduits of feeding rather than mere places of worship, and clerics unknowingly surrender fragments of themselves through devotion. Horundar’s ocean becomes one of the largest reservoirs of this consumption, where drowned souls are absorbed into the Deep Hunger, their essence circulating through tidal currents before being claimed into his immortal reservoir. His conflicts with other gods are often territorial disputes over mortal populations and coastal dominion, where control over worship determines access to sustenance.

The broader pantheon reflects a fractured hierarchy of divine predation. Valkhamesh governs storms and authority from celestial thrones, Enkirael feeds upon war and bloodshed, Raeshkul shapes strategy and civilization, Nefarokir governs death and the underworld, and Asethyr consumes ecstasy and madness. Each god represents a different mode of hunger, but Horundar remains uniquely tied to total environmental consumption, where entire geographies become mechanisms of sacrifice. Even in rivalry or restraint, his influence persists through water itself, ensuring that no coastal civilization exists outside his reach.

Beneath all divine order lies the ancient terror of Thoryn-Rahek, the first great hunger and devourer beneath creation. In the Colossus Wars, Thoryn-Rahek nearly unmade existence itself, consuming divine and mortal civilizations alike until the surviving gods bound him within the deepest fractures of reality. This act of imprisonment fundamentally changed the pantheon, transforming their hunger from instinct into fear-driven necessity. Immortality became something that required constant feeding, or else collapse into oblivion would follow.

Roughly four centuries before the present age of Universal, mortal civilizations united in secret to overthrow divine domination. Industrial powers, arcane orders, naval coalitions, royal houses, and revolutionary movements collaborated to construct the Age of Containment. Across the continent, massive metaphysical vault-prisons were forged beneath mountains, oceans, deserts, and forgotten ruins. These prisons did not kill the gods but confined them within sealed realms where their ability to consume mortal essence was heavily restricted. Twenty-one seals were created, each tied to a specific deity, transforming divine power into a regulated and dangerous resource rather than an unchecked force.

The seals imposed catastrophic feedback whenever a god attempted excessive consumption, turning divine feeding into pain that even immortals could not ignore indefinitely. Yet the gods still remain active, capable of granting spells, visions, and limited influence through carefully monitored systems of worship. Civilization did not escape divinity but replaced open divine rule with controlled dependency. Skyships, rail networks, and portal systems all rely on regulated divine energy, making humanity both liberated from gods and structurally dependent upon them at the same time.

Within this modern world, Horundar continues to manifest through storms, maritime disasters, and psychic influence over those who travel across the seas. Sailors report visions of drowned kingdoms, collapsing coastlines, and endless depths that whisper with collective memory. Naval routes are treated as negotiations with a living god rather than neutral geography, and entire fleets are still offered in ritualized protection against his wrath. His influence persists not only in physical disaster but in the psychological certainty that the ocean is watching, remembering, and waiting.

Universal itself is a civilization built upon contradiction, where divine imprisonment created stability while simultaneously embedding dependence upon the very forces it sought to control. Humanity overthrew the gods yet continues to rely upon fragments of their power to sustain industry, travel, and communication. Horundar remains one of the most dangerous pillars of this system because his domain cannot be fully separated from mortal infrastructure. Every river, sea route, and coastal settlement exists within his inherited design, meaning that even in containment, he remains one of the most pervasive forces shaping the world.
public_lore: Horundar rules oceans, storms, floods, earthquakes, flame, stone, air, and the raw force that breaks settled boundaries. Coastal kingdoms treat survival as conditional upon his mood and their continuing rites of appeasement.
common_worship: Invoked by sailors, coastal rulers, elemental practitioners, miners, farmers awaiting rain, and communities threatened by flood, drought, quake, or storm.
religious_warning: Horundar’s protection is territorial and temperamental. A calm sea may be permission rather than peace.
public_origin_record: No reliable mortal record explains what this being was before the age of divine rule. Temple accounts, forbidden histories, and prison records contradict one another.

pantheon_source.document_summary: A narrative pantheon compendium preserving each deity’s domains, manifestation, divine character, and sacred history.

canon_authority.authority_rule: The canonical 22-god order and dedicated creator compendium govern every deity-to-people relationship; province and settlement placement does not alter divine parentage or race canon.

created_races.family_description: Elemental and Energy-Born Peoples contains the canonical parent races Genasi, Elemental Kin, Elementborn, and Panolima. Genasi has four bloodlines, Elemental Kin has two, Elementborn has six, and Panolima has five bundled custom bloodlines. All of these ancestries remain under Horundar's single creator category.
created_races.creation_doctrine: Canonical race-compendium doctrine: Horundar holds this single creator category through storms, seas, earthquakes, floods, flame, stone, air, and raw elemental force. The canonical parent races are Genasi, Elemental Kin, Elementborn, and Panolima. Genasi has four bloodlines, Elemental Kin has two, Elementborn has six, and Panolima has five bundled custom bloodlines. Temple language preserves reverence, but its colder margins classify each race, bloodline, lineage, and form by yield, pressure, environment, devotion, fear, beauty, endurance, and the particular note it awakens in the god's appetite.
created_races.created_peoples_record: Horundar is recorded as the single creator-god of the Elemental and Energy-Born Peoples category: Genasi, Elemental Kin, Elementborn, and Panolima. Genasi has four bloodlines, Elemental Kin has two, Elementborn has six, and Panolima has five bundled custom bloodlines. The public hymn calls this lineage and blessing; the older register reads like curated divine husbandry, sorting bodies, habitats, temperaments, and spirit-resonance so storms, seas, earthquakes, floods, flame, stone, air, and raw elemental force never depends on one mortal pattern alone.

parent_races.name: Genasi
parent_races.description: Genasi are elemental humanoids whose mortal bodies express a clear elemental ancestry. In Universal, Genasi are one parent race with Air, Earth, Fire, and Water lineages rather than four unrelated top-level races. In older divine registers, this people is catalogued by habitat, temperament, resilience, and resonance.

canonical_subtypes.name: Air Genasi
canonical_subtypes.description: Born of living wind and storm currents, Air Genasi bodies often feel lighter than they should be and are naturally attuned to altitude and motion. They are frequently seen as distant or restless, as if always partially elsewhere in the sky. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

canonical_subtypes.name: Earth Genasi
canonical_subtypes.description: Forged from stone, metal, or deep earth pressure, Earth Genasi possess dense, enduring bodies that resist harm and hardship. They are typically steady and patient, valuing permanence and reliability above change. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

canonical_subtypes.name: Fire Genasi
canonical_subtypes.description: Touched by living flame, Fire Genasi often carry warmth in their presence and sometimes literal embers within their form. They are intense and driven, prone to passion that can either inspire or destroy. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

canonical_subtypes.name: Water Genasi
canonical_subtypes.description: Shaped by tide and current, Water Genasi bodies flow with subtle adaptability and can endure pressure others cannot. They are emotionally fluid and deeply responsive to surrounding energies and environments. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

parent_races.name: Elemental Kin
parent_races.description: Elemental Kin are humanoid peoples whose bodies lean toward a living elemental state without being Genasi or Panolima. In standard selection, Flamekin and Rimekin are bloodlines under this parent race. In older divine registers, this people is catalogued by habitat, temperament, resilience, and resonance.

canonical_subtypes.name: Flamekin
canonical_subtypes.description: Small, volatile beings of concentrated fire essence, Flamekin flicker with unstable inner heat that reflects their emotions. They are quick to act and quick to burn out if not tempered. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

canonical_subtypes.name: Rimekin
canonical_subtypes.description: Born of frost and glacial energy, Rimekin carry cold within their bones and often leave traces of ice in their wake. They are calm and detached, valuing control and restraint. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

parent_races.name: Elementborn
parent_races.description: Elementborn are people shaped by a dominant environmental or elemental birth-state. In Universal, Ashborn, Azureborn, Bogborn, Deepborn, Snowborn, and Stoneborn are lineages of one Elementborn parent race. In older divine registers, this people is catalogued by habitat, temperament, resilience, and resonance.

canonical_subtypes.name: Ashborn
canonical_subtypes.description: Created from volcanic ash and elemental aftermath, Ashborn embody both destruction and rebirth. They are survivors who adapt quickly to devastation and change. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

canonical_subtypes.name: Azureborn
canonical_subtypes.description: Infused with stormlight and arcane sky-energy, Azureborn shimmer with faint electric or luminous traits. They are curious and analytical, often drawn to patterns in chaos. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

canonical_subtypes.name: Bogborn
canonical_subtypes.description: Shaped by stagnant wetlands and decaying elemental mire, Bogborn thrive in toxicity and slow, heavy environments. They are patient, secretive, and highly resilient in adverse conditions. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

canonical_subtypes.name: Deepborn
canonical_subtypes.description: Born from abyssal pressure and deep elemental convergence, Deepborn are adapted to crushing depths and silence. They are introspective and often perceive reality in slow, layered ways. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

canonical_subtypes.name: Snowborn
canonical_subtypes.description: Manifested from persistent winter cycles and frozen wind, Snowborn carry the stillness of long cold seasons. They are disciplined and emotionally restrained, but deeply enduring. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

canonical_subtypes.name: Stoneborn
canonical_subtypes.description: Hardened from living rock and continental force, Stoneborn bodies are near-immovable and highly durable. They are grounded thinkers who prefer stability and long-term planning. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

parent_races.name: Panolima
parent_races.description: Living Embodiments of Elemental Harmony: Earth, Fire, Water, Air, and Aether. In older divine registers, this people is catalogued by habitat, temperament, resilience, and resonance.

canonical_subtypes.name: Earth Bloodline
canonical_subtypes.description: You gain a climbing speed of 20 feet on stone, trees, cliffs, or earthen surfaces. You have advantage on checks made to detect unstable ground, structural weaknesses, mineral deposits, or hidden natural passages. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

canonical_subtypes.name: Fire Bloodline
canonical_subtypes.description: You gain resistance to fire damage. You can shed bright light in a 10-foot radius and dim light for an additional 10 feet. Once per long rest, when you deal fire damage, you may add your proficiency bonus to one damage roll. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

canonical_subtypes.name: Water Bloodline
canonical_subtypes.description: You gain a swimming speed equal to your walking speed and can breathe air and water. You ignore movement penalties from nonmagical currents, mud, ice, or shallow water. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

canonical_subtypes.name: Air Bloodline
canonical_subtypes.description: Your walking speed increases by 5 feet. When you jump or fall, you may glide up to 20 feet horizontally and reduce falling damage by five times your level. You have advantage on checks involving wind, storms, pressure changes, or airborne sounds. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.

canonical_subtypes.name: Aether Bloodline
canonical_subtypes.description: You gain resistance to force damage from environmental magical surges or arcane storms. At 3rd level, you may cast detect magic once per long rest. At 5th level, you may cast misty step once per long rest, appearing as a pulse of elemental light. Temple marginalia marks this as a tuned lineage expression rather than a separate act of mercy.
